```{r}
# ---- Export figures to the journal submission folder -------------------------
# Set save_figs <- FALSE to render the manuscript without re-writing the files.
save_figs <- TRUE

fig_out_dir <- file.path(
  "/Users/Anthony/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-UW/University of Washington",
  "Writing and Drafting/All Study Area SOC/Submission/JGRB/Revision2/Figures"
)
if (save_figs) dir.create(fig_out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Saves a ggplot/patchwork object at the same dimensions used in the chunk
# options (fig-width, fig-height, fig-dpi) so the exported file matches the
# manuscript figure exactly.
save_fig <- function(plot, name, width, height, dpi = 300, formats = "png") {
  if (!save_figs) return(invisible(NULL))
  out <- file.path(fig_out_dir, paste0(name, ".", formats))
  for (i in seq_along(formats)) {
    ggplot2::ggsave(
      filename = out[i],
      plot = plot,
      width = width,
      height = height,
      units = "in",
      dpi = dpi,
      bg = "white"
    )
  }
  invisible(out)
}

# Copies a figure that is embedded as a static image (![...](Figures/*.png))
# into the same submission folder under its figure number.
copy_fig <- function(from, name) {
  if (!save_figs) return(invisible(NULL))
  from <- here("writing", from)
  dest <- file.path(fig_out_dir, paste0(name, ".", tools::file_ext(from)))
  file.copy(from, dest, overwrite = TRUE)
  invisible(dest)
}
```

```{r}
      ),
```

## Key Points

1.  The distribution of soil carbon stocks across Pacific Northwest landscapes is driven by wetland presence
2.  Digital soil mapping using random forest outperformed linear mixed models for soil carbon stocks across wetlands and uplands
3.  Wetland probability did not correspond to the carbon concentration in mineral soils

\pagebreak

## Abstract

Inland freshwater wetlands are poorly mapped and represented despite disproportionately storing soil organic carbon (SOC) relative to their surface area. Here, we assess if digital soil mapping models improve by adding a spatially-continuous wetland probability, the Wetland Intrinsic Potential, WIP, as a predictor for SOC stocks and SOC across both wetlands and uplands in heterogeneous landscapes. We collected soil samples in four watershed study areas across the Pacific Northwest and evaluated both linear mixed models and quantile random forest models to predict SOC stock (g cm^-2^) distribution and mineral soil SOC (SOC %) concentration. The quantile random forest model with WIP as a predictor was the best performing and most accurate model for SOC stocks. However, WIP was not included in models for mineral SOC % in the mineral soil. Instead, edaphic factors including depth, pH, and clay content were primary predictors of mineral SOC %, consistent with the well-known accumulation of coarse, particulate organic material in wetlands. Using the best performing SOC stock model, we mapped SOC stocks across the four watersheds with scaled up estimates of mean wetland SOC stocks of 114-243 Mg C ha^-1^ compared to mean upland SOC stocks of 99.5-162 Mg C ha^-1^. The differences between wetland and upland SOC stocks were contrasted in comparison of new model maps to current SOC stock maps from an ensemble of global and region models. This study demonstrates how incorporating probabilistic wetland maps can show wetland-driven patterns of large SOC stocks contained in organic soils.

## Plain Language Summary

Freshwater wetlands store about 30% of the world's soil carbon even though they only cover 6-8% of land. However, wetlands are often missing from maps, making it hard to understand where carbon is stored. In this study, we tested if creating new wetland maps could help us better predict where soil carbon is found. Our results showed that the wetland map was important for predicting total carbon storage, it ranked as the third most important factor after soil depth and climate. We found that wetlands stored much more carbon than upland areas with 114-243 megagrams of carbon per hectare, while uplands averaged 99.5-162 megagrams per hectare. Our mapping approach captured small scale differences in carbon storage related to wetlands better than existing methods, while still giving similar estimates for total landscape carbon. However, the wetland map didn't help predict carbon concentrations in deeper mineral soils, only in the organic surface layers. For mineral soils, factors like depth, pH, and clay content were more important predictors. These findings show that we need to include wetlands in carbon mapping and consider how different factors control carbon at different soil depths.

\pagebreak

## Introduction

Soil organic carbon (SOC) is the largest terrestrial carbon pool and a key dynamic reservoir in the carbon cycle, with uncertain responses to climate change [@scharlemann2014; @varneyEvaluationSoilCarbon2022]. The immense size of the SOC pool has raised concern for the potential positive feedback of carbon released back to the atmosphere [@bradfordManagingUncertaintySoil2016]. However, SOC is not uniformly distributed across landscapes and can be largely influenced by patterns of inland freshwater wetlands (hereafter shortened to "wetlands") which contain large SOC stocks in organic rich soils [@siewertHighresolutionDigitalMapping2018; @larsonSoilMoistureControls2023; @stewartRevealingHiddenCarbon2024]. Wetlands maintain disproportionately high SOC stocks per unit area compared to non-wetlands or uplands, accounting for approximately 30% of the global SOC pool while occupying only 6-8% of the terrestrial surface area [@jacksonEcologySoilCarbon2017; @poulterReviewGlobalWetland2021]. Therefore, capturing the spatial patterns of wetlands is central to accurately representing spatial distributions of SOC.

Digital Soil Mapping (DSM) is a primary approach to capture the distribution of soil characteristics such as SOC across spatial extents ranging from landscapes to regional and global scales [@minasnyChapterOneDigital2013]. DSM uses geospatial predictors as proxies for soil formation and development, often applying the "SCORPAN" [@mcbratneyDigitalSoilMapping2003] approach which adapts the original soil formation equation from @jennyFactorsSoilFormation1941 to model a soil property as a function of predictors representing other soil characteristics (S), climate (C), organisms (O), topography (R), parent material (P), time/age (A), and spatial location (N). DSM uses these SCORPAN predictors in geostatistical models such as kriging to machine learning models such as Random Forest at progressively applying to finer spatial resolutions [@khaledianSelectingAppropriateMachine2020; @minasnyDigitalSoilMapping2016]. DSM is often applied towards modeling SOC stocks by modeling SOC concentration (SOC % by mass, e.g. g g^-1^) and bulk density (g cm^-3^) then multiplying them with a depth interval (cm) to calculate SOC stock on a per area basis (g cm^-2^) [@poggioSoilGridsProducingSoil2021; @chenDigitalMappingGlobalSoilMap2022]. Additionally, SOC stock can be calculated from SOC % and bulk density in pre-processing a dataset in specific depth intervals then modeled using SCORPAN predictors [@vitharanaFactorsControllingSpatial2024]. Further assessing the contribution of each SCORPAN predictor can reveal drivers of SOC accumulation with land cover classes and vegetation remote sensing indices representing the organisms (O) in SCORPAN are often having high importance [@lamichhaneDigitalSoilMapping2019].

Yet, DSM still faces some challenges in modeling both SOC stocks or SOC %. In particular, despite advances in wetland mapping, many wetlands are still hidden or missing, leading to mis-classification as uplands or another non-wetland type [@wickhamThematicAccuracyAssessment2021; @sjogerstenTropicalWetlandsMissing2014]. Many current SOC sampling designs and large-scale synthesized datasets used in DSM omit organic horizons or exclude histosols, focusing specifically on the mineral soil and omitting large amounts of carbon in surface organic layers [@heitkamp2021; @georgiouGlobalStocksCapacity2022; @poggioSoilGridsProducingSoil2021]. This lack of representation of carbon-rich wetland soils can contribute to disagreement among several different DSM products in their estimates of SOC % across organic soil horizons compared to mineral soil layers [@feeney2022]. Furthermore, using currently available wetland maps and datasets shows that wetland SOC stock, as well as the proportion of total landscape SOC held in wetlands are potentially greatly underestimated [@stewartRevealingHiddenCarbon2024].

While wetland presence can correspond to large SOC stocks and potentially improve DSM models [@larsonSoilMoistureControls2023], its effectiveness as a predictor in more complex models across larger scales and different locations is uncertain. A growing approach to improve wetland spatial representation, especially under forest vegetation, is to model a land surface as a continuous probability corresponding to wetland presence or water inundation using fine-resolution topography data [@maxwell2016; @delanceyLargescaleProbabilisticIdentification2019; @halabiskyWetlandIntrinsicPotential2023; @zhangDevelopmentGlobalDataset2021]. Yet, there has been seldom inclusion of a probabilistic wetland indicator as a model predictor of SOC stock or SOC % outside of single watershed scale studies [@stewartRevealingHiddenCarbon2024]. Moreover, it is uncertain how wetland probability would fair as a predictor compared to other SCORPAN predictors in both DSM and non-DSM models, the latter of which do not use statistical inference to predict soil properties across a landscape from environmental predictors. Non-DSM models statistically infer driving factors of soil variables and can more easily adapt intrinsic soil predictors such as soil pH, clay content, and mineral type while still incorporating spatial variables such as mean annual precipitation and temperature or drainage class [@minasnyDigitalSoilMapping2016]. Several studies use this modeling approach to examine controls on SOC % in the mineral soil which consistently documents intrinsic soil properties like Fe and Al concentrations or particle size as drivers [@georgiouDivergentControlsSoil2021; @heckmanBulkDensityFractions2021; @nave2021; @vonfrommControlsRelationshipsSoil2024; @wiesmeierSoilOrganicCarbon2019]. However, wetland soils are rarely represented in these studies and there is a need to establish how explicit wetland presence can affect SOC % with other predictors in a complex model.

In this research, we assess if, and to what magnitude, a probabilistic map of wetland presence acts as an important predictor in DSM models of SOC stock with SCORPAN predictors and non-DSM models of mineral SOC % with intrinsic soil properties across different climatic regions in the Pacific Northwest. We examined the wetland probability importance within simpler linear mixed models and more complex machine learning models to elucidate predictor variable importance and model prediction accuracy changes for SOC stock in the entire soil profile and and SOC concentration (%) in the mineral soil. Both model types were used with and without the wetland probability predictor allowing us to assess drivers of SOC stock and mineral SOC %. We also compared mapped estimates of landscape-level SOC stocks from our best performing model to SOC maps derived from larger regional scales. <!--# Probably add some detail -->

## Methods

### Study Areas

![Map of study watersheds in the Pacific Northwest of North America. The Heen Latinee Experimental Forest (HLEF) is located in Southeast Alaska. The Hoh River Watershed (HRW), Mashel River Watershed (MRW), and Colville Valley Watershed (CVW) are located in Washington State. The size of the red dots is proportional to the size of the inset circle for each study area. Map lines delineate study areas and do not necessarily depict accepted national boundaries](Figures/PNW_Study_Areas.png){#fig-studymap fig-align="center" width="6.5in"}

\pagebreak

We conducted field surveys, sample collection, and geospatial modeling across four study watersheds in the Pacific Northwest that stratify a climatic gradient ([@fig-studymap]). The Heen Latinee Experimental Forest (HLEF) is located in Southeast Alaska near Juneau, AK with a mean annual precipitation (MAP) of approximately 2284 mm and a mean annual temperature (MAT) of 4.3 ˚C. The Hoh River Watershed (HRW) is located on the west coast of the Olympic Peninsula where MAP is approximately 3061 mm and MAT is 10.0 ˚C. The Mashel River Watershed (MRW) is located on the western side of the Cascade Mountain Range near Tahoma (Mt. Rainier) and has a MAT of 8.4 ˚C and a MAP of approximately 1716 mm. The Colville Watershed (CVW) is located on the northeastern portion of the state and has a MAT of 6.5 ˚C and a MAP of 652 mm. The landscapes of the four study areas contain a range of landforms including mountains, hillslopes, alluvial floodplains, and glacial moraines and outwash plains. Geologic ages range from late Quaternary deposits from retreating glaciers in the HLEF and HRW, Oligocene-Eocene volcanic and sedimentary rocks in the MRW to Pre-Tertiary metamorphic rocks in the CRW. Vegetation is predominantly forested with the HLEF containing a mix of Western Hemlock (*Tsuga heterophylla*), and Sitka Spruce (*Picea sitchensis*) with small amounts of Yellow Cedar (*Cupressus nootkatensis*). The HRW forests contain Sitka Spruce, Western Hemlock, Western Red Cedar (*Thuja plicata*), and Bigleaf Maple (Acer macrophyllum). The MRW forests contain predominantly Douglas fir (*Pseudotsuga menziesii*), Western Hemlock, and Red Alder (*Alnus rubra*). The CVW forests contain a mix of Ponderosa Pine (*Pinus ponderosa*), Douglas fir, Lodgepole pine (*Pinus contorta*), Western Larch (*Larix occidentalis*), Western Hemlock, and Western Red Cedar.

### Wetland Identification with the Wetland Intrinsic Potential (WIP) Tool

We implemented the Wetland Intrinsic Potential (WIP) tool for each study watershed to model the gridded land surface in each study area as a continuous probability of wetland presence, with each grid pixel containing a value from 0-100% [@halabiskyWetlandIntrinsicPotential2023]. The WIP tool relies on multi-scale terrain metrics derived from digital terrain models (DTMs) as predictors of wetland presence on the landscape which has been shown to improve wetland classification [@maxwell2016; @maxwell2019]. These terrain metrics include slope, curvature, and deviation from mean elevation calculated at 50-1000m scales. Additional single scale terrain metrics included topographic wetness index [@beven1979] and topographic depth to water. Additional remote sensing metrics representing wetland identifiers included normalized difference wetness index, normalized difference vegetation index, and canopy height. Training data used for wetland presence and absence were derived from the National Wetland Inventory (NWI) through a randomized sample of areas inside and outside wetland polygons with a 3:1 non-wetland (upland) to wetland ratio. Small riverine wetlands were excluded from this sampling. The Random Forest model [@breimanRandomForests2001] with NWI training data and predictors then estimates a probability value (0-1.0, revised to 0-100% for interpretability) for each pixel based on a "wetland" or "upland" designation. We follow @halabiskyWetlandIntrinsicPotential2023 and others in using a probability threshold of ≥ 50% to define the cutoff for defining a wetland (≥50%) or upland (\<50%). In the random forest model, the percentage (e.g. ≥50%) represents the proportion of statistical decision trees that have classified the observation location as wetland. The 50% cutoff can be set higher or lower, but @halabiskyWetlandIntrinsicPotential2023 found that 50% was optimal for balancing omission and commission errors. However, we noted in the Supplementary Materials (Supplementary Table 2.) <!--# Supplementary Table -->that the higher commission error in the CVW could indicate over-estimates of total wetland area. Yet, to be consistent across the four study areas, we maintained the ≥50% threshold for determining wetland presence. We utilized both the data and framework of the HRW WIP implementation to derive similar WIP models for the HLEF, MRW, and CRW study watersheds. More detailed methods describing the WIP implementation, including the variable importance for WIP (Supplementary Figure 1. and Supplementary Table 1.) <!--# Supplementary Table --> is located in the Wetland Intrinsic Potential tool section of the Supplementary Materials.

### Field sampling and laboratory analysis

Soil samples were collected over the course of two field summer field seasons in 2021-2022. Sample locations were pre-selected using a stratified random selection of points across the WIP probability for each study watershed in order to evaluate the full spread of the wetland-upland gradient. The WIP probability from 0-100% was stratified into 30 equal size bins and sample points were generated for those bins at random locations within each study watershed. Sample locations were then visited in the field as close to the sample point coordinates as possible and then updated with new GPS/GNSS location data. Overall we collected samples from 114 pedon locations with 30 pedons each in the MRW and CVW, 36 pedons in the HRW, and 18 pedons in the HLEF. The HLEF also contained 3 legacy soil pedons sampled in 2019. Soil pedons were dug to at least 1m depth unless there was a restrictive layer. Soil pedons were characterized according to NRCS field sampling guides [@soilsurveystaffFieldBookDescribing2024] and soil samples for bulk density and bulk chemistry were extracted by horizon and at the horizon center. Laboratory analysis started with drying samples to a constant weight at 70˚C and sieving to 2mm to remove coarse fragments. The mass of the \< 2mm fraction was then used to calculate bulk density and analyze carbon content, particle size distribution, and pH. Carbon content was measured using an Elemental Analyzer (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan). Particle size distribution was measured using the hydrometer method. Soil pH was measured using 1:1 soil to water ratio, although a small number of soils required 1:1.5 or 1:2 soil to water

### Geospatial data

Geospatial datasets were gathered to determine predictors for SOC stocks across the three study areas. We chose geospatial factors related to vegetation, climate, lithology and geology, and topography. For vegetation spectral indices, we used Google Earth Engine @gorelickGoogleEarthEngine2017 to obtain satellite imagery from Sentinel-2. We calculated each index for the month of August, representing peak growing season, for each year from 2018 to 2023, then took the median value across those years. In particular, for each study area we calculated enhanced vegetation index (EVI) [@hueteOverviewRadiometricBiophysical2002] and normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI). Other metrics such as the soil adjusted vegetation index (SAVI) were also investigated but deemed too correlated to either NDVI or EVI to be included in the model. We also used a lidar derived canopy height model from the Washington Department of Natural Resources (WA DNR) which was measured as the elevation difference between the lidar DTM and the lidar digital surface model.

For climate predictors, we downloaded 800m^2^ gridded 30 year climate normals for mean annual precipitation (MAP) and mean annual temperature (MAT) from the Northwest Alliance for Computation Science and Engineering PRISM Climate @prismclimategroup30YearNormals for all four study watersheds. In addition, we also downloaded Potential Evapotranspiration (PET) from the Version 3 of the Global Aridity Index and Potential Evapotranspiration Database for all four study areas [@zomerVersion3Global2022]. PET was divided by MAP to create an Aridity Index estimate of water availability similar to the Global Aridity Index in @zomerVersion3Global2022. To capture finer scale effects of solar radiation and heat, we calculated a heat load index (HLI) from the lidar DTM [@mccuneEquationsPotentialAnnual2002].

Geology and lithology maps were downloaded from the Washington Department of Natural Resources at a 1:100,000 scale and from the USGS [@wilsonGeologicMapAlaska2015]. These maps contained a wide range of mapped geologic and lithologic categories, often combining with geomorphologic processes. We chose to consolidate them into six broad categories which would represent soil Parent Material (PM) and time since soil inception: Glacial Till and Drift, Glacial Outwash, Igneous, Metamorphic, Sedimentary, and Unconsolidated sediments. More details are provided in the PM section of the Supplementary Materials and Supplementary Table 2<!--# Supplementary Table -->.

### Modeling approach

#### Data structure

Our approach consisted of separating our data into two datasets: one for SOC stocks by equal depth intervals and another for mineral SOC % using the original depth measurements. This split was due to the removal of organic horizons to target the mineral SOC %. For the SOC stock dataset we utilized a DSM approach to transform our SOC stock data into equal intervals of 25cm using a mass preserving spline depth function [@chenDigitalMappingGlobalSoilMap2022; @obrienMpspline2MasspreservingSpline2022]. We use the assumption that depth is a continuous variable and its relationship with SOC is captured with the mass preserving spline at all locations in our study areas. While glacially-influenced landscapes can have high variability in structure across soil depth, the spline approach allows us to also include depth as a predictor and we can make predictions of SOC at a specified depth interval at any location in our study areas [@maPredictingSoilProperties2021a]. This approach is common in DSM and has been referred to as 3-D because it facilitates the prediction of soil properties at any location within the study area at the designated depth intervals [@helfensteinThreedimensionalSpaceTime2024; @maloneMappingContinuousDepth2009; @bishopModellingSoilAttribute1999]. The decision to use 25cm intervals instead of the standardized intervals was to control the variability and limit any potential inflation of the the number of observations for SOC stock within the depth interval thickness. Additionally, we correct for soil volume across profile depths by subtracting the coarse fragment or rock % by volume of the sample horizon before calculating SOC stocks. The 25cm intervals maintained a similar number of observations without exceeding the original dataset (Original: 573, Spline 499). We used the mass preserving spline function to calculate values of SOC %, Bulk Density, and Rock % down profile using a lambda = 0.7. These numbers were then used to calculate SOC stocks for each 25cm depth interval by [@eq-SOC-stock-spline]:

$$Spline\,SOC_{g\,cm^{-2}} = Spline SOC_{\%} * Spline BD_{g\,cm^{-3}}*25cm*(1- Spline Rock_{\%})$$ {#eq-SOC-stock-spline}

For the mineral SOC % dataset, we removed observations that were heavily organic based on the @soilsurveystaffKeysSoilTaxonomy2022 organic soil definition of \> 12% SOC. However, we also chose a more conservative threshold of \>10% SOC to remove potential high organic matter soils which would affect the further lab analyses. We use mineral SOC % from here on to make a distinction from overall SOC % that might include organic horizons and to investigate intrinsic soil properties measured only in the mineral soil. We note that this should not be confused with mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM) which is measured with particular methods The analyses for these samples consisted of measurements of sand, silt, clay, and pH with distributions shown in Supplementary Figure 2<!--# Supplementary Figure -->. Measurements of sand, silt, clay, and pH were not mapped and therefore, we did not use this dataset for digital soil mapping and therefore kept the original depth intervals from the field sampling. This dataset contained 426 observations compared to the 499 in the spline dataset and 573 in the original dataset.

#### Model Building and Selection

We used only geospatial predictors for SOC stock to produce spatially explicit maps without having to model additional edaphic factors from the laboratory and field sampling analysis. However, we combined both geospatial and edaphic factors for predicting mineral SOC %. We note that other modeling approaches can take advantage of covariance between multiple dependent variables [@babcock2013], but this was beyond the scope of our current research objectives. In @tbl-soc-predictors we show the final selection of variables used in both models.

##### Linear Mixed Modeling

We chose to use two model types in our research to model SOC stock and SOC %: a linear mixed effects model (LM) and a quantile random forest (RF). We chose to use a LM approach to test specific hypotheses about important predictors and examine predictor coefficients. To compare between models, both datasets for SOC stock and SOC % were split into training and testing datasets using a 85:15 ratio. The same training and testing datasets were used for all models to compare performance and accuracy. Models were also compared with and without the WIP predictor.

In the LMMs, the sample location was chosen as a random effect and sample depth was specified as a random slope within the sample location. We chose to build several models that represented our a priori hypotheses with varying interactions between the predictors as well as eliminating predictors that were not significant down to a null model with no predictors. The final model was chosen using Akaike's information criterion (AIC) and parsimony then evaluated for violations of homogeneity of variance and linearity. Although some observations deviated slightly from the homoscedasticity assumption (Supplementary Figure 3 and 4)<!--# Supplementary Figure -->, we deemed the model assumptions sufficiently met and therefore used to evaluate drivers and predict SOC stock and SOC %.

All data used to build models of SOC stock and SOC % were centered and scaled using the base R function `scale` if they were continuous predictors. Correlated variables were removed if they had an r \> 0.6. However, at this scale MAP and PET:MAP are highly correlated and thus we used separate models to assess the strength between the two predictors in our mixed model selection. The initial model selection process using maximum likelihood showed that models using PET:MAP instead of MAP were better fits to the data according to AIC.

For SOC stock, LM selection using AIC comparisons removed models containing interactions among fixed effects, resulting in SOC stock modeled as a function of PET:MAP, WIP, Canopy Height, Heat Load Index (HLI), PM, and Depth as fixed effects @eq-model-1 :

$$SOC\,stock\,_{ij} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{_{ij}}MAT + \beta_{_{ij}}PET:MAP + \beta_{_{ij}}WIP + \beta_{_{ij}}CanopyHeight + \beta_{_{ij}}PM + \beta_{_{ij}}Landform + \beta_{_{ij}}Depth + b_{0_{j}} + b_{{ij}}Depth + \epsilon_{ij}$$ {#eq-model-1}

For mineral soil SOC %, the LM selection process was similar to SOC stock where fixed effects in separate models were removed depending on the AIC values. The best LM at this stage contained depth, pH, clay, and PET:MAP with interactions between the variables the latter three predictors. After this LM was found, we also used the `dredge` function from the `MuMIn` R package to further identify if incorporated interactions between clay % or silt+clay% and MAT outperformed the current LM structure determined from earlier [@bartonMuMInMultimodelInference2023]. The final LM was chosen with the lowest AIC and/or fewest LM parameters for parsimony with PET:MAP, pH, clay% and Depth as fixed effects @eq-model2 :

$$SOC\,\%\,_{ij} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{_{ij}}PET:MAP + \beta_{_{ij}}Clay\% + \beta_{_{ij}}pH +  \beta_{_{ij}}pH:(PET:MAP) + \beta_{_{ij}}Depth + b_{0_{j}} + b_{{ij}}Depth + \epsilon_{ij}$$ {#eq-model2}

All random effects in the LM followed:

$$b_{0j} \sim N(0, \sigma^{2}_{b_{0}}) $$ {#eq-model3}

$$b_{_{ij}}Depth\sim N(0, \sigma^{2}_{b_{Depth}}) $$ {#eq-model4}

$$\epsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^{2}) $$ {#eq-model5}

Where $b_{0j}$ is the random intercept for the $j$-th group of each sample location and $b_{_{ij}}Depth$ is the random slope of depth within the sample location. The final model was evaluated on the test dataset by measuring the R^2^ and root mean square error (RMSE). Predictor variable importance was estimated using the 95% confidence intervals on the scaled coefficient estimates with important predictors having a confidence interval that did not cross 0.

We also examined SOC stock data and model residuals for spatial autocorrelation by examining semivariograms and the spatial autocorrelation within each study watershed expecting there to be minimal autocorrelation. There was some spatial pattern in the MRW but none in the other three watersheds shown by the semivariograms within and across all study watersheds (Supplementary Figure 5)<!--# Supplementary Figure -->. We concluded that our proposed model structure did not need to include a spatial autocorrelation random effect although this has been shown to be beneficial in mapping SOC [@mckenzieSpatialPredictionSoil1999].

##### Random Forest Modeling

The Quantile Random Forest (RF) was used to accommodate for potential non-linear relationships in our data as well as incorporate a more flexible approach to predictor selection. We used the `mlr3` package in `R` to implement the RF from the `ranger` package [@wrightRangerFastImplementation2017; @mlr3]. We used recursive feature elimination to narrow the number of predictors used in the model. Then, we tuned `num.trees` (1000), `mtry` (4), and `max.depth` (8), using repeated 10-fold cross validation on the training dataset. Out of bag (OOB) R^2^ and RMSE were calculated from the model implemented on the training dataset. We calculated R^2^ and RMSE for the RF on the test dataset similar to the LMM. Predictor variable importance was determined using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values using a 200 observation subset of the training dataset as the rows to be explained and the full training dataset as the background [@lundbergUnifiedApproachInterpreting2017]. SHAP values were visualized using the `kernelshap` package [@mayerKernelshapKernelSHAP2024]. We also investigated interactions between predictors in the RF using the interpretable machine learning `iml` package @molnar2018iml and the `Interaction` function [@molnar2018iml].

#### SOC stock prediction and uncertainty

Mapped predictions of SOC stock across all four study watersheds were made using the model with the best fit to the test dataset (R^2^ and RMSE), which resulted in the RF that included the WIP predictor. This model was used to generate SOC predictions for each depth interval (25cm) and then combined to calculate a 1m SOC stock as well as the 97.5% and 2.5% quantiles of SOC stock to show uncertainty the range.

We also used additional geospatial masks to remove permanent surface water areas and urban zones. The Modified Normalized Difference Water Index (MNDWI) was used to remove permanent surface water such as lakes and large rivers with a threshold of 0.3 [@xuModificationNormalisedDifference2006]. The National Land Cover Database (NLCD) was used to mask urban areas such as roads, which can be confused with water or other hydrologic features [@dewitzNationalLandCover2021]. Geospatial masks using the WIP threshold of ≥ 50% for wetlands and <50% for uplands were used to estimate wetland and upland 1m SOC stocks and were compared with 1m SOC stock data from the National Wetland Condition Assessment (NWCA) which was upscaled using the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) in @uhranImprovedWetlandSoil2021. We show these estimates using the the term NWCA~NLCD~.

We also extracted estimates of SOC stock from open data sources that have been used to model the spatial distribution of SOC at regional to global scales. For all study areas, we used an estimated mean 1m SOC stock from an ensemble combination of global and regional models compiled and calculated by @jonesEnsembleModelInput2024 for Alaska, British Columbia, Washington, Oregon, California, and Hawai'i. Additionally, a published map of 1m SOC stocks was created specifically for the Pacific Coastal Temperate Rainforest by @mcnicolLargeClimatesensitiveSoil2019 which encompasses the HLEF.

## Results

### Wetland identification with the Wetland Intrinsic Potential (WIP) tool

```{r}
#| include: false

ta <- c(11019, 64538, 21434, 32118)
wa <- c(2188, 5798, 2184, 862)
wa/ta
```

Wetland mapping conducted with the Wetland Intrinsic Potential (WIP) Tool ( [@fig-PNW-WIP-Maps; @halabiskyWetlandIntrinsicPotential2023]) and setting the wetland classification threshold at ≥ 50% identified considerably more wetland area than the National Wetland Inventory (NWI) (Supplementary Table 2). Overall accuracy for the WIP models including both wetland and non-wetland identification was 87% in the HLEF, 92% in the HRW, 90% in the MRW, and 93% in the CVW. Wetland omission error was 15%, 14%, 12%, and 2% while wetland commission error was 10%, 11%, 6%, and 20% for the HLEF, HRW, MRW, and CVW, respectively. The largest percentage increase of wetland area identified occurred in the HLEF (155%) and the lowest occurred in the HRW (50.1%). HLEF had the largest relative wetland extent proportionally to the total watershed extent (20%) while the CVW had the lowest total and proportional wetland extent (2.7%). The most important variables for these models included mostly terrain metrics such as gradient and deviation from mean elevation at various scales (See Methods for explanations on multiscale terrain metrics; Supplementary Figure 1). <!--# Supplementary Figure -->

### Variation across study areas along climatic gradient

Overall, SOC stocks were larger at shallow depths and smaller at deeper depths across the four study areas [@tbl-mean_stdev_stocks_table]. We observed low SOC stocks (mean = 0.26, range 0.07-0.69 g cm^-2^ in the CVW and high SOC stocks in the HLEF (mean = 0.77, range = 0.43-1.24 g cm^-2^). The largest SOC stocks were mostly in the HLEF with proportionally more deep SOC in the 125-150cm depth interval compare to other study areas. Mineral SOC % was more evenly distributed across wetlands and uplands after applying 10% SOC % concentration threshold to remove organic soil horizons from the original dataset and reduced the number of wetland observations in each study area \[See Methods for mineral SOC % threshold explanation; (Supplementary Table 4)<!--# Supplementary Table -->. Overall mineral SOC % was highest in the HRW upland soils (mean = 4.25%) and was nearly twice as high compared to the HRW wetland soils (mean = 2.75%). The next highest mineral SOC % were found more evenly distributed between wetlands and uplands in the MRW, HLEF, and CVW, respectively.

### Performance of models for SOC stock and mineral SOC %

```{r}
#| label: in_text_lmm
#| include: false


best_dredge_model_R2list <- readRDS(here("writing/in_text_values/best_dredge_model_R2list.rds")) |> 
    base::round(2)
best_dredge_model_R2list 
best_dredge_model_R2list_noWIP <- readRDS(here("writing/in_text_values/best_dredge_model_R2list_noWIP.rds")) |> 
    base::round(2)
best_dredge_model_R2list_noWIP

qrf_errdf <- read.csv(here("data/dataframes/MLR3_RFM_ErrorDF.csv")) |> dplyr::mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ base::round(.x , 2)))
qrf_errdf |> flextable::flextable()

qrf_errdf_nw <- read.csv(here("data/dataframes/MLR3_RFM_ErrorDF_noWIP.csv")) |> dplyr::mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ base::round(.x , 2)))
qrf_errdf_nw |> flextable::flextable()
```

The linear mixed model (LM) for predicting SOC stocks accounted for 49% of the variability in the training dataset with a R^2^~marginal~ of `r best_dredge_model_R2list["lmmMargR2"][[1]]` for the fixed effects and R^2^~conditional~ of `r best_dredge_model_R2list["lmmCondR2"][[1]]` including the random effects of sample location with depth ([@tbl-model-stats]). The However, in the test dataset, the LM accounted for a much lower proportion of the variation with an R^2^ = `r best_dredge_model_R2list["lmmTestR2"][[1]]` and had higher variability with an RMSE = `r best_dredge_model_R2list["lmmTestRMSE"][[1]]` [@fig-predact-graph]. Separating the uplands and wetlands based on the ≥ 50% WIP threshold in the test dataset revealed the LM had better prediction for the upland SOC stocks (R^2^ = `r best_dredge_model_R2list["lmmTestR2upl"][[1]]`, RMSE = `r best_dredge_model_R2list["lmmTestRMSEupl"][[1]]` g cm^-2^) compared to the wetlands (R^2^ = `r best_dredge_model_R2list["lmmTestR2wet"][[1]]`, RMSE = `r best_dredge_model_R2list["lmmTestRMSEwet"][[1]]` g cm^-2^). The LM without WIP was similar to the LM with WIP but with higher test R^2^ on the uplands and lower test R^2^ in the wetlands. In contrast to the LMM, the quantile random forest model (RF) had a lower R^2^ = `r qrf_errdf$RFM.R2_OOB[1]` and comparable RMSE = `r qrf_errdf$RFM.RMSE_OOB[1]` g cm^-2^ when using the out of bag (OOB) data from the training dataset. The RF outperformed the LM on the test dataset with an R^2^ = `r qrf_errdf$RFM.R2_test[1]` and RMSE = `r qrf_errdf$RFM.RMSE_test[1]` g cm^-2^. The RF also predicted the the uplands test data (R^2^ = `r qrf_errdf$RFM.R2_test[3]`, RMSE = `r qrf_errdf$RFM.RMSE_test[3]` g cm^-2^) better compared to the wetland test data (R^2^ = `r qrf_errdf$RFM.R2_test[2]`, RMSE = `r qrf_errdf$RFM.RMSE_test[2]` g cm^-2^), with both predictions better fits than the LM. The RF without WIP also had similar performance to the full RF model on the training dataset but under-performed on the test dataset, and in particular for both wetlands and uplands.

Important predictors for predicting SOC stock the LM and RF containing all parameters consistently included Depth (@fig-varimp A.). Depth was the strongest predictor in the LM with the largest absolute coefficient value and was negatively associated with SOC stock (`r Depth_est`). The LM for SOC stock also included an interaction between Depth and WIP (Supplementary Figure 6)<!--# Supplementary Figure -->, but this effect was not significant (`r depthwip_est`). Additionally the LM identified the PET:MAP climatic variable (`r petmap_est`), Landforms, and Parent Material (PM) categories as the next most important predictors. Landforms in the LM with significant negative associations for SOC stock were Flat (`r flat_est`) and Spur (`r spur_est`). The PM categories of Sedimentary (`r sed_est`) and Unconsolidated (`r unc_est`) both had significant negative associations with SOC stock. The WIP was a significant positive predictor in the model (`r wip_est`) along with Canopy Height (`r chm_est`). The LM without WIP also excluded Canopy Height, but other predictors remained consistent (@fig-varimp C.).

In the RF for SOC stocks, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values were highest for Depth (`r depth_shap`) then followed by several variables within close proximity to each other, indicating comparable variable importance after Depth ([@fig-varimp B.]). These included WIP with the second highest SHAP value (`r wip_shap`), PET:MAP as the third highest SHAP value (`r petmap_shap`), and MAP as the fourth highest (`r map_shap`). Predictors after MAP in terms of SHAP value were MAT, Elevation, PM, and Canopy Height. Without WIP in the RFM, predictors were similar except that Landform was included above PM and Canopy Height (@fig-varimp D.).

SHAP dependence plots, showing the effects of predictors on model predictions (e.g. positive or negative effect on predicting SOC stocks) showed WIP was positively related to SOC stocks, mostly above 75%, but that this did not vary by study area although the CVW had fewer observations with WIP above 75% [@fig-shap-pdp, A.]. Model predictions had a much stronger relationship with depth, with near surface soils having positive SHAP values and soils below 50cm having mostly negative SHAP values (model predicts lower SOC stock) [@fig-shap-pdp B.]. High WIP values combined with low PET:MAP resulted in positive model predictions but SHAP values were much lower, around 0.1 compared to other predictor effects [@fig-shap-pdp C.]. According to the interaction strength measured by Friedman’s H-statistic, WIP in the RF for SOC stock showed high interaction values (H~statistic~ ≥ 0.2) with PET:MAP, Landform, and the Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI). PET:MAP in turn had a high interaction with WIP but also with the other climate variables, MAP and MAT (Supplementary Figure 7)<!--# Supplementary Figure -->. Depth, was the largest individual predictor but showed little interaction strength (H~statistic~ ≤ 0.1) with other variables compared to other predictors.

For mineral SOC %, Both the LM and RF had consistent agreement for important predictors, identifying Depth, pH, and clay as the top three, while excluding the WIP predictor ([@fig-varimp C. & D.]). Depth had the highest LM coefficient and RF SHAP value (`r Depthlab_est` & `r depthlab_shap`), consistent with the SOC stock models. pH showed a significant effect on mineral SOC %, which decreased as mineral soil became more neutral indicated by the negative coefficient estimate in the LM (`r ph_est`) and high SHAP value in the RF (`r ph_shap`). clay % had a positive coefficient in the LM (`r clay_est`) and high SHAP value in the RF (`r clay_shap`).

SHAP dependence plots showed SHAP values had a strong decline with mineral SOC with depth and pH [@fig-shap-pdp D. & E.]. Similar to SOC stock, mineral soils \<50cm from the surface were predicted to have higher mineral SOC% [@fig-shap-pdp D.]. Clay % was mostly a positive influence on model predictions of mineral SOC % [@fig-shap-pdp E.]. Combined with pH, high Clay % soils with acidic pH (pH below 5) were also predicted to have higher mineral SOC % and Clay % seemed to decline slightly with increasing pH and SHAP values, potentially indicating an interaction [@fig-shap-pdp E.]. The LM identified a specific interaction between pH and the climate variable PET:MAP (`r petmap_ph_est`) with the decline in mineral SOC % as a function of pH (Supplementary Figure 6)<!--# Supplementary Figure -->. Similar to the RF for SOC stocks, Depth again had lower interaction values with other predictors except for pH (H~statistic~ ≤ 0.1). Consistent with the LM for mineral SOC %, the RF also estimated that pH had a large interaction PET:MAP (H~statistic~ ≥ 0.2). Clay % had stronger interactions overall compared to Depth and pH but with correlated variables such as silt+clay and sand. The interaction between clay and MAP and PET:MAP was also strong (H~statistic~ ≥ 0.2).

### Upscaling SOC stock estimates across watershed study areas

```{r}

#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-show: hold
#| tbl-cap: Table of soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks derived from the mapping the quantile random forest across the four study watersheds (HLEF, HRW, MRW, and CVW). Additional published estimates are added here for comparison. The mapped 1m SOC stock from Jones and D'Amore, 2024 are derived from an ensemble of global models for the Pacific Northwest region and extracted for each study watershed. Wetland areas for Jones and D'Amore 2024 were derived by aggregating the WIP probability maps to 60m resolution and considering the coverage of pixels with WIP values greater than 50% probability as wetlands. Currently available mapped estimates of wetland 1m SOC stock are for CONUS are provided by Uhran et al., (2021) using the data from the National Wetland Condition Assessment (NWCA) and the National Land Cover Database (NLCD).
```

\pagebreak

The RF for SOC stocks including the WIP was used to upscale estimates 1m SOC stocks across the full extent of the four study watersheds (HLEF, HRW, MRW, and CVW) based on its fit to the test dataset to upscale the observations of SOC stocks ([@fig-ensemble-map-compare]). The RF also predicted uncertainty intervals using the 2.5^th^ and 97.5^th^ quantiles which were then summarized in Supplementary Table 6<!--# Supplementary Table -->. We calculated that the HRW had the largest SOC stock of `r tbl_socmap2$body$dataset$Total_SOC_Tg[3]` Tg due to its large areal extent compared to other watersheds ([@tbl-socmap2]). The highest mean SOC stocks predicted by the RF model were in the HLEF with a mean of `r tbl_socmap2$body$dataset$AverageSOC_Mgha[1]` Mg ha^-1^. We estimated the lowest total SOC stocks in the HLEF (`r tbl_socmap2$body$dataset$Total_SOC_Tg[1]` Tg), which coincides with a small relative area compared to other watersheds. The lowest mean SOC stock was estimated in the CVW (`r tbl_socmap2$body$dataset$AverageSOC_Mgha[7]`). SOC stock patterns in the CVW appeared more homogenous compared to other study areas, consistent with less wetland area according to WIP. Across all study areas, wetlands delineated by using the WIP probability threshold of greater than 50% showed consistently higher upscaled SOC stocks compared to the overall mean and non-wetland upland SOC stocks.

An ensemble mean of global and regional models for the PNW region [@jonesEnsembleModelInput2024] showed 1m SOC stocks varied with broad similarly to our estimates across the four watersheds ([@tbl-socmap2]). The ensemble combination of global models from Jones and D'Amore, 2024 had slightly higher but comparable estimates for total 1m SOC stocks in the HLEF, MRW, and CVW with higher mean SOC stocks and larger areas. However, we estimated substantially less total SOC in the HRW at `r tbl_socmap2$body$dataset$Total_SOC_Tg[3]` TgC compared to `r tbl_socmap2$body$dataset$Total_SOC_Tg[4]` TgC in Jones in D'Amore, 2024 ([@fig-ensemble-map-compare]). We used the same WIP map with a threshold of 50% wetland probability to define wetlands in both the ensemble maps and our SOC maps. We saw small differences in wetland extent due to the differences in resolution (60m in Jones and D'Amore 2024, 4-5 m in our maps). For wetlands defined by the WIP, our estimates of mean SOC stocks were slightly higher than Jones and D'Amore, 2024 for the HLEF and for the HRW but lower for wetlands in the MRW and CVW. Mean and total wetland SOC stock estimates from this study and Jones and D'Amore, 2024 were higher than upscaled mean and total wetland SOC estimates from the National Wetland Condition Assessment and the National Land Cover Database (NWCA) published by @uhranImprovedWetlandSoil2021. However, estimated mean and total upland SOC stock from Jones and D'Amore, 2024 were much higher than our estimates. There is a notable difference for mean and total upland SOC stock for the HRW between our estimates and Jones and D'Amore, 2024.

## Discussion

Improving the spatial representation of inland freshwater wetlands is crucial for capturing landscape patterns of SOC stocks and can enhance further modeling of landscape carbon cycling and the implementation of natural climate solutions [@bossioRoleSoilCarbon2020; @bradfordManagingUncertaintySoil2016]. Digital soil mapping (DSM) using soil forming factors from the SCORPAN (S: soil, C: climate, O: organisms, R: relief, P: parent material, A: age, N: location) framework is a prominent approach to generating accurate maps of soil parameters like SOC [@minasnyChapterOneDigital2013]. Integrating probabilistic wetland mapping using tools such as the Wetland Intrinsic Potential tool into DSM can identify hidden wetlands especially under forested canopy [@halabiskyWetlandIntrinsicPotential2023] as well as provide a continuous predictor for modeling of both wetland and upland SOC [@stewartRevealingHiddenCarbon2024]. Our research showed that integrating the WIP as a predictor worked best in a random forest model (RF) compared to a linear mixed model (LM) where WIP helped predict large SOC stocks. The LM models discounted WIP as a predictor and even with excluding WIP were able to account for nearly 50% of the training dataset variation. But both LM models performed poorly on the test dataset with an R^2^ = 0.18-0.20 The RF including WIP for SOC stocks accounted for 50% of the test dataset variability compared to 46% in the non-WIP RF. This led to greater confidence in producing SOC stock maps which showed larger SOC stocks in wetland locations than another DSM SOC stock product. However, we found that models generated robust predictions of mineral SOC % without the WIP predictor, instead relying on edaphic factors such as Depth, pH, and clay.

### Incorporating wetland probability as a SOC predictor in digital soil mapping

DSM for SOC is frequently challenged by landscapes that span different climate regimes, vegetation communities, and complex topography [@minasnyChapterOneDigital2013] which is further compounded by unmapped wetlands often hidden by forested canopy with potentially high SOC stocks [@davidson2022]. The WIP tool can successfully identify forested wetlands with lidar-derived multi-scale terrain indices, producing a probabilistic output which captures the landscape gradient of uplands to wetlands [@halabiskyWetlandIntrinsicPotential2023; @langEnhancedDetectionWetlandStream2012; @maxwell2016]. The WIP wetland probability has the potential to also identify landscape processes related to wetland presence, such as increasing soil moisture and subsequent soil carbon accumulation [@larsonSoilMoistureControls2023]. However, using a probabilistic map of wetlands as a predictor for SOC stocks has rarely been implemented beyond a watershed within a single climatic zone [@stewartRevealingHiddenCarbon2024]. At larger regional scales, climate variables such as precipitation and temperature and biome classification can be the most significant predictors of SOC stock [@wiesmeierSoilOrganicCarbon2019]. Our analysis in four watersheds across the Pacific Northwest using models with climate and vegetation indices with and without WIP probability, showed that a RF model with WIP had the highest prediction accuracy. Moreover, we show that the WIP probability was a slightly larger significant predictor of SOC stock compared to climate and vegetation indices, but well below depth.

Yet, simply including the WIP as a predictor in DSM is not a silver bullet for modeling SOC stocks. The improvement of the WIP addition was approximately a 5% increase in test R^2^ compared to the model without WIP. Additionally, there was still high variability in the upper end of our SOC stock predictions and still approximately 50% of the variation left unexplained in our test dataset.The RF with WIP under-predicted large SOC stocks in MRW wetlands [@fig-predact-graph downward triangles] and did not distinguish SOC stock patterns corresponding to wetland areas in the CVW [@fig-ensemble-map-compare]. These patterns in the two drier study areas (MRW and CVW) might indicate that climate factors were still strongly affecting the predictions of SOC stocks in wetland soils or that we may need additional predictors for SOC stocks beyond our current suite of predictors. For example, at the watershed scale more explicit forest community or vegetation metrics that differentiate hydric, mesic, and xeric plant communities or classification wetland classification information such as Hydrogeomorphic classes could help identify carbon accumulation areas [@daugherty2019; @goyette2024; @wiesmeierSoilOrganicCarbon2019]. @chizenDriversSoilCarbon2025 found that wetland class explained the largest amount of variability in the Prairie Pothole region and @pearseSoilOrganicCarbon2018 showed that SOC stock can vary widely between different wetland types and vegetation cover. Incorporating the variation within a wetland different wetland classes as continuous probabilities, similar to peatland probabilities in other previous research [@helfensteinThreedimensionalSpaceTime2024; @delanceyLargescaleProbabilisticIdentification2019].

It is well known to DSM practicioners that improvements to wetland maps would benefit DSM for SOC stocks. @henglAssessmentSoilOrganic2023 used topography-derived hydrologic variables and lithological maps to represent potential wetland and wet areas in a DSM approach in Alberta, Canada but found that wetland SOC stocks were underestimated due to resolution. @waldenMultiscaleMappingAustralias2023 used DSM for blue carbon and terrestrial carbon stocks incorporating a multi-resolution decomposition of topographic wetness index (TWI) to improve Australia's national carbon inventory but indicated inland freshwater wetland ecosystems were included under terrestrial categories. The regional ensemble model by @jones2024 used 11 different DSM sources, where some used implicit and explicit wetland data which we have noted have difficulty distinguishing small wetlands [@feeney2022]. Wetland inventories and maps used by larger regional scale models can benefit from updating via remote sensing technology and more advanced geospatial modeling [@wulder2018] and there has been growing research incorporating modeled wetland data into SOC predictions. @helfensteinThreedimensionalSpaceTime2024 more directly used peatland occurrence maps as predictors for SOC and further developed dynamic peatland occurrence maps over time between 1953 and 2022 to more accurately estimate changes in SOC. Although not wetland-specific, @larsonSoilMoistureControls2023 used a similar approach to our WIP wetland probability by including a predictor variable from a separate machine learning model designed to capture probabilistic soil moisture which was further used to accurately map SOC and tree biomass. Future DSM approaches for SOC stock can continue to improve wetland representation using explicit modeling for wetland presence.

### Drivers of SOC stocks across scales

Depth as the largest significant predictor in both LM and RF models for SOC stock was largely expected since SOC stocks typically decline with depth [@jobbagyVerticalDistributionSoil2000] and there were no other spatially-explicit predictors that accounted for SOC stock variation within the pedon. Our modeled SOC stocks likely reflect the realistic decreases in SOC stock with depth across these watersheds, however, these predictions should be cautiously interpreted due to the high variability with soil structure (e.g. coarse fragment and root content; shallow bedrock) along the soil profile. This variation is likely implied in model predictions but ~in-situ~ observations can differ due to these soil structure characteristics. Using depth as a predictor in a DSM approach has been termed "3D" mapping [@poggioNationalScale3D2014; @sotheLargeScaleMapping2022]. But our approach differs slightly by applying a "2.5D" DSM method using the mass-preserving spline function to harmonize our dataset observations across 25cm depth intervals [@maloneMappingContinuousDepth2009; @obrienMpspline2MasspreservingSpline2022]. The advantages with our approach allowed us to maintain the original dataset variation without inflating observations. Additionally, we limited the influence of large depth intervals on SOC stocks and obtained a negative exponential decline of SOC stock with Depth. This allowed our approach to use Depth as an effective predictor similar to "3D" DSM but with the mass-preserving spline of "2.5D" DSM. Our modeled SOC stocks across 

After Depth, many of the largest predictors of SOC stock in both the LM and RF included large scale climatic variables, primarily PET:MAP and MAT. Climatic variables are a significant large scale factor in the original soil formation equation [@jennyFactorsSoilFormation1941] and the SCORPAN framework [@chenDigitalMappingGlobalSoilMap2022; @feeney2022; @minasnyChapterOneDigital2013; @minasnyDigitalMappingPeatlands2019]. In particular, water availability climatic predictors such as PET:MAP and MAP have been shown to outweigh temperature predictors such as MAT on overall SOC stocks [@vonfrommControlsRelationshipsSoil2024; @hobleyDriversSoilOrganic2015; @jobbagyVerticalDistributionSoil2000]. Wetlands need persistent water saturation to maintain their high SOC stocks [@maGloballyRobustRelationship2022]. However, temperature has been shown to have a greater effect on SOC held in organic horizons or composed in coarse particulate forms [@georgiouEmergentTemperatureSensitivity2024; @garcía-palacios2024] and this can be pronounced in cooler climates such as the Pacific Northwest [@mcnicolLargeClimatesensitiveSoil2019]. Since wetlands tend to accumulate SOC tends in near-surface organic horizons as particulate organic matter, a combination of moisture decline and temperature rise could significantly impact wetland SOC stocks [@quan2025]. Previous research has shown that higher temperatures can stimulate decomposition in wetland and peatland organic soils [@hribljanElevationTemperatureAre2023; @fellmanVulnerabilityWetlandSoil2017]. In addition to the RF model ranking PET:MAP as a significant predictor, partial correlation analysis showed wetland SOC distinguished by the WIP was negatively associated with MAT (Supplementary Table 5)<!--# Supplementary Figure -->.

The RF included WIP as a significant predictor of SOC stock, showing that higher probabilities of inundated or saturated soils led to larger SOC stocks in the landscape. The LM for SOC stocks discounted the WIP predictor and performed worse on the test dataset. The lower performance of the LM was could be due to the interactions and non-linear relationships between SOC stock and WIP. Above 75% WIP was where the largest increases in SOC stocks occurred [@fig-shap-pdp A.]. This was similar to the non-linear soil moisture model in @larsonSoilMoistureControls2023 that predicted SOC stocks. The RF was able to accommodate for these relationships and produce higher predictive performance compared to the LM. Conspicuously, both models discounted explicit vegetation parameters such as Canopy Height, or EVI, with early model iterations also excluding vegetation type classification. This is consistent with larger scale findings that biological drivers may lag behind bio-climatic and edaphic predictors for SOC stocks [@yuClimaticGeochemicalControls2021; @wangUpscalingSoilOrganic2024]. However, future modeling should still seek more sufficient ways to represent vegetation communities that could improve modeling SOC stocks.

### Drivers of mineral soil SOC %

Unexpectedly, both models were able to capture majority of the variability for mineral SOC % across both wetlands and uplands without WIP unlike the models for SOC stock. This could be attributed to the aggressive 10% carbon content cutoff used to remove organic horizons and examine the mineral soil specifically, along with additional non-spatial soil edaphic predictors. Our methods were used to gain insight into factors controlling SOC within soil horizons that might be associated with minerals and protected [@georgiouGlobalStocksCapacity2022]. Although we did not thoroughly examine the diverse array of soil parameters that drive mineral SOC %, the lack of WIP in the final LM and RF indicate climatic and edaphic drivers of mineral SOC % are more significant than landscape-scale variables across the different regions. In particular, the landscape-scale WIP predictor appears to be more sensitive to organic matter accumulation near the surface in our study area's wetlands. However, our models did not replicate previous research in mineral soil wetlands without organic horizons that show SOC % declines going from frequently saturated to rarely saturated mineral soils [@kottkampPhysicalProtectionAggregates2022; @tangenSoilOrganicCarbon2020]. Furthermore, we did not incorporate the study design from both @kottkampPhysicalProtectionAggregates2022 and @tangenSoilOrganicCarbon2020 that thoroughly examined individual wetlands with sampling along transects whereas our sample locations were spread across each watershed. We acknowledge that intra-wetland SOC variability can be large [@stewartSettingReferenceWetland2023] and forested wetlands need a robust evaluation which could utilize a study design similar to @tangenSoilOrganicCarbon2020 where wetland-upland transect sampling for SOC % and edaphic factors are replicated across multiple individual wetlands and climatic regions.

In our study, the main drivers of mineral SOC % were primarily Depth, PET:MAP, pH, and clay. The Depth LM coefficient and SHAP value was not markedly larger than pH, the next largest significant predictor. This is consistent with previous research across continental scales, where pH and Depth accounted for large proportions of the variability in SOC % [@yuClimaticGeochemicalControls2021]. @nieStorageControllingFactors2023 also showed that pH played a major role in wetland SOC stocks and influenced effects from vegetation and climate which corresponds with our partial correlation (Supplementary Table 5)<!--# Supplementary Table --> that showed that wetland SOC % was more sensitive than upland SOC % to pH and clay %. Clay % was the next largest predictor in terms of coefficient and SHAP value which is also consistent with a long history of research showing that higher clay % is associated with higher SOC % [@jobbagyVerticalDistributionSoil2000]. However, the relationship is not as clear in wetland soils. @kottkampPhysicalProtectionAggregates2022 found bulk SOC % was not related to clay % but instead found that macroaggregates promoted more SOC storage. More detailed analysis in wetland soils has indicated a diverse array of factors that drive SOC % including the presence of metals [@liuMetallicProtectionSoil2024]. @dongFactorsControllingSoil2022 found that Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC) and Bulk Density were the largest predictors of SOC %. However, both CEC and Bulk Density measurements are often functions of SOC % and it is misleading to interpret that it is driving SOC % [@rossCationExchangeForest2008]. For this reason, we also did not consider Bulk Density in our study as a driver for mineral SOC % and focused on the particle size and pH, although it is often useful to use BD as proxy for SOC %.

Interactions between climate and soil factors, particularly geochemistry, have been well studied in recent years, with strong evidence that both groups play significant roles in SOC % [@doetterlSoilCarbonStorage2015; @rasmussenClayImprovedSet2018; @yuClimaticGeochemicalControls2021]. Measuring geochemical factors such as Fe and Al oxides would likely provide more nuance to controlling predictors in our study and should be considered in future SOC research. Moreover, contemporary soil science research has shifted focus towards on the mineral-associated vs. particulate fractions which illuminate potential responses to climate change [@heckmanBulkDensityFractions2021; @rocciSoilOrganicCarbon2021]. Many uncertainties remain about the driving factors of mineral-associated and particulate SOC, but this research area should also include wetland soils to more comprehensively understand the overall terrestrial carbon cycle.

\pagebreak

## Conclusions

Our research shows a DSM approach using an RF model was moderately improved by integrating the WIP wetland probability compared to both LM with WIP and another RF model without WIP. The WIP probability was an important predictor in the RF over climatic and vegetation factors but there was still approximately 50% of variability remaining in the test dataset. We consider the WIP wetland probability as a driver of SOC accumulation in particulate organic matter at the soil surface, a key characteristic of many wetlands. However, WIP was not a predictor of mineral SOC % where drivers were a mix of edaphic and climate predictors. While our study is limited in examining all potential factors driving mineral soil SOC % beyond pH and particle size, these results should motivate a more comprehensive SOC assessments across both terrestrial-aquatic environments to enhance our understanding of SOC distribution across landscapes. Future research should continue to refine wetland probabilistic modeling and investigate potential uses for other landscape function such as greenhouse gas fluxes or groundwater hydrology.
